source_en: An Eligible GDHCN Participant is one of the following: • a WHO Member State or Associate Member, or sub-national unit thereof; • a State Party to the International Health Regulations (2005), or sub-national unit thereof; • the United Nations (UN) and other intergovernmental organizations in effective relations with WHO; • a fund, programme, specialized agency, or related organization within the UN system; or • an organization officially delegated by one of the organizations mentioned above that can abide by the GDHCN Terms of Participation and fulfils one or more of the following health service functions: • Public Health Agency; • Health Professions Education Accreditation Agency; • Health Services Licensing Agency; or • Public Health Security Agency. and, once accepted to the GDHCN, after the successful conclusion of the Onboarding Process, will be referred to as GDHCN Participant throughout this document. source_en: An entity that stores, signs, and issues cryptographic certificates and certifies the ownership of a public key by the named subject of the certificate. This allows GDHCN Trust Network Gateway participants to rely on signatures or assertions made in relation to the private key corresponding to the certified public key. Certificate Authorities may be operated by different types of entities, including, but not limited to, a private-sector Certificate Authority, a ministry or agency responsible for ICT/eGovernment services, a Ministry of Health, or another competent authority within the jurisdiction. It is the responsibility of each GDHCN Participant to determine the appropriate arrangement for its Certificate Authority, in accordance with applicable laws and policies within its jurisdiction, to guarantee security and proper data management. Each GDHCN Participant must identify, establish, or liaise with the relevant Certificate Authority, as applicable and impose on the latter all requirements of this document.
back_translation_en: Entity that stores, signs and issues cryptographic certificates and certifies that the public key belongs to the subject named in the certificate. This allows participants in the GDHCN Trust Network Gateway to rely on signatures or assertions made by means of the private key corresponding to the certified public key. Certificate Authorities may be operated by different types of entities, including, without being limited to, a private-sector Certificate Authority, a ministry or agency responsible for ICT/e-government services, a Ministry of Health or another competent authority of the jurisdiction. It is incumbent on each GDHCN Participant to determine the appropriate arrangement for its Certificate Authority, in accordance with the laws and policies applicable in its jurisdiction, in order to guarantee security and appropriate data management. Each GDHCN Participant must, as the case may be, designate or set up the competent Certificate Authority, or liaise with it, and impose on it all the requirements of this document.

source_en: Digital signatures can be used to achieve data integrity and authenticity. Public Key Infrastructures establish trust by binding public keys to verified identities (or issuers). This is necessary to allow other participants to verify the data origin and the identity of the communication partner and decide about trust. In the TNG, multiple public key certificates are used for authenticity. This document defines which public key certificates are used and how they should be designed in order to allow broad interoperability between the different GDHCN Participants. This document is based on [[ehn-trust-framework-2021]](en/folio-assistant-core/bibliography/#ref-ehn-trust-framework-2021) and [[ehn-dcc-techspec-vol1-2021]](en/folio-assistant-core/bibliography/#ref-ehn-dcc-techspec-vol1-2021). It provides more details on the necessary public key certificates and it gives guidance on certificate templates and validity periods for countries that want to operate their own SCA. Since DSCs shall be verifiable for a defined time-frame (starting from the issuing, expire after a given time), it is necessary to define a verification model for all signatures applied on the public key certificates and the digital health certificate. Legal and administrative procedures are not in the scope of this document, they must be defined separately.
back_translation_en: Digital signatures can serve to guarantee the integrity and authenticity of data. Public key infrastructures establish trust by binding public keys to verified identities (or issuers). This is necessary to allow other participants to verify the origin of the data and the identity of the counterpart, and to decide on their trust. In the TNG, several public key certificates are used for authenticity. This document defines which public key certificates are used and how they should be designed in order to allow broad interoperability between the different GDHCN Participants. This document builds on [[ehn-trust-framework-2021]](en/folio-assistant-core/bibliography/#ref-ehn-trust-framework-2021) and [[ehn-dcc-techspec-vol1-2021]](en/folio-assistant-core/bibliography/#ref-ehn-dcc-techspec-vol1-2021). It provides more details on the necessary public key certificates and gives guidance on certificate templates and validity periods for countries that wish to operate their own SCA. Given that DSCs must be verifiable during a defined period (from their issuance, they expire after a given duration), it is necessary to define a verification model for all signatures applied to public key certificates and to the digital health certificate. Legal and administrative procedures are outside the scope of this document; they must be defined separately.

source_en: The trust model of the GDHCN framework is a Public Key Infrastructures (PKI). Each GDHCN Participant maintains one or more Signing Certificate Authority (SCA), certificates of which are relatively long lived. The SCA issues public key certificates for the short lived, Document Signers (i.e. signers for digital health certificates), which are called Document Signer Certificates (DSCs). The SCA acts as a trust anchor such that relying GDHCN Participants can use the SCA certificate to validate the authenticity and integrity of the regularly changing DSC certificates. Once validated, the GDHCN Participant can provide these certificates (or just the public keys contained therein) to their validation applications.
back_translation_en: The trust model of the GDHCN framework is a public key infrastructure (PKI). Each GDHCN Participant manages one or more signer certification authorities (SCA), whose certificates have a relatively long lifetime. The SCA issues public key certificates for short-lived document signers (that is, the signers of digital health certificates), called document signer certificates (DSC). The SCA acts as trust anchor, so that the GDHCN Participants relying on it can use the SCA's certificate to validate the authenticity and integrity of the DSC certificates, which change regularly. Once these certificates are validated, the GDHCN Participant can provide them (or only the public keys they contain) to its validation applications.

source_en: → The creation of a digital PHR following vaccination for each individual may incentivize more people to participate in a public health measure (e.g. receive a vaccine) to access the benefits of a digital PHR. However, it may also increase hesitancy to participate in the public health measure because of privacy and other concerns that the vaccination record could be linked to personal data and be used for functions other than those originally intended (e.g. surveillance of individual health status), or be used by unintended third parties (e.g. immigration, commercial entities, researchers) [royal-society-setc-vaccine-passports-2021].
back_translation_en: → The creation of a digital PHR following the vaccination of each person may encourage more people to participate in a public health measure (for example getting vaccinated) in order to access the benefits of a digital PHR. However, it may also increase reluctance to participate in the public health measure, because of privacy concerns and other concerns about the fact that the vaccination record could be linked to personal data and used for purposes other than those initially intended (for example monitoring individual health status), or be used by unintended third parties (for example immigration services, commercial entities, researchers) [royal-society-setc-vaccine-passports-2021].

source_en: A number of further possible uses for digital PHRs raise ethical issues. In the context of a public health emergency, a digital PHR might play a role in achieving various public health purposes such as determining vaccination coverage in a given population, which may help to determine when to lift or relax public health and social measures (PHSMs) at a population level. A digital PHR might also be used to facilitate individualized exemption from, or, reduction of PHSMs (e.g. reduced quarantine time post exposure) or individual access to an activity based on proof of vaccination (if such uses are held to be ethical), which we can term a “health pass” function. The potential deployment or utilization of a digital PHR for these purposes, particularly as a health pass, engenders a number of potential ethical problems for individuals and communities, and human rights challenges ([coe-bioethics-vaccine-pass-2021],[who-vaccination-certificates-ethics]).
back_translation_en: A number of other possible uses of digital PHRs raise ethical questions. In the context of a public health emergency, a digital PHR could play a role in achieving various public health objectives, such as determining vaccination coverage in a given population, which can help determine when to lift or relax public health and social measures (PHSM) at the population level. A digital PHR could also be used to facilitate an individualized exemption from PHSM or their reduction (for example a reduced quarantine duration after an exposure), or individual access to an activity on the basis of proof of vaccination (if such uses are deemed ethical), which may be called a "health pass" function. The potential deployment or use of a digital PHR for these purposes, in particular as a health pass, gives rise to a number of potential ethical problems for individuals and communities, as well as human rights issues ([coe-bioethics-vaccine-pass-2021],[who-vaccination-certificates-ethics]).

source_en: Third, a digital PHR in its use as a health pass risks introducing unfair disadvantages and injustices. For example, during the COVID-19 PHEIC, the initially limited supply of COVID-19 vaccine within some countries had been distributed to prioritize those at greatest risk of infection (such as health-care workers) or severe outcomes (such as the elderly).  There is a danger that those who are willing to be vaccinated but have not yet been offered a vaccine, or those who are unable to be vaccinated for medical reasons, would be unfairly disadvantaged if a digital PHR incorporated health pass functions. Consideration should be given to whether individuals could use other proofs of health status to allow them similar access to the same services while mitigating the risk of disease spread. For example, during the COVID-19 PHEIC, these other proofs may have included a negative COVID-19 test or proof of post-infection-acquired immunity based on tests that are reliable and accurate (which have been called immunity certificates), although this also raises considerable scientific and ethical concerns [voo2021].

Together, these are called Participants. Some aspects in this document must be coordinated between the Participants, such as the management of a namespace and the distribution of cryptographic keys. It is assumed that one party, hereinafter referred to as the Secretariat, performs these tasks. source_en: The Digital TRUST Infrastructure for Discovery and Validation (Regi-TRUST) is a DNS-based decentralized trust management infrastructure that bridges the gap between different certificate ecosystems and enables trust interoperability. Regi-TRUST's "network of networks" model allows ecosystems of trusted digital services operated by various stakeholders to securely publish service endpoints collated with their independent governance policies and with support for root of trust architectures to allow interoperable verifications. Implementers of Regi-TRUST can leverage tools provided to create purpose-sized networks of trusted digital services operated by all types of entities, using lightweight infrastucture and technical governance due to the decentralized federation approach. Regi-TRUST was originally started by the Linux Foundation in 2021 as the Global COVID-19 Certificate Network (GCCN), and is now sponsored and hosted by the United Nation Development Programme (UNDP).
back_translation_en: The Digital TRUST Infrastructure for Discovery and Validation (Regi-TRUST) is a decentralized DNS-based trust management infrastructure, which bridges the gap between different certificate ecosystems and enables trust interoperability. Regi-TRUST's "network of networks" model allows trusted digital service ecosystems operated by various stakeholders to securely publish service endpoints attached to their independent governance policies, with support for root-of-trust architectures to enable interoperable verifications. Regi-TRUST implementers can take advantage of the provided tools to create appropriately sized trusted digital service networks, operated by all types of entities, using lightweight infrastructure and technical governance thanks to the decentralized federation approach. Regi-TRUST was originally launched by the Linux Foundation in 2021 under the name Global COVID-19 Certificate Network (GCCN), and is now sponsored and hosted by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

source_en: Currently EU DCC Gateway is a single centralized system which establishes trust between DCC participants and enables the sharing of business rules, value sets and revocation lists. If another region in the world establishes such a gateway, there is currently no method in the architecture to exchange these trusted data between the two gateways. In this new architecture within the DDCC context, multiple gateways can be connected to each other and share trusted data. In the long term, this architecture will allow the creation of groups and ultimately the establishment of a federation. Such an architecture may be applicable and of interest for non-authority parties e.g. airlines, which desire a read only copy of the gateway content. This can be established by onboarding the airline in a gateway specially setup for this purpose and is connected to the official gateway. To achieve this goal, the architecture must support multiple operation modes e.g. Primary-Secondary. The current implementation of EU DCCG is, as mentioned before, a single centralized system which serves as a hub for storing and managing the necessary information gathered from the Trusted Parties.
back_translation_en: Currently, the EU DCC gateway is a single centralized system that establishes trust between DCC participants and enables the sharing of business rules, value sets and revocation lists. If another region of the world establishes such a gateway, there is currently no method in the architecture to exchange this trust data between the two gateways. In this new architecture, in the DDCC context, several gateways can be connected to each other and share trust data. In the long term, this architecture will allow the creation of groups and, ultimately, the establishment of a federation. Such an architecture may be applicable and of interest to non-institutional parties, e.g. airlines, that wish to have a read-only copy of the gateway's content. This can be achieved by onboarding the airline into a gateway specially set up for this purpose and connected to the official gateway. To achieve this objective, the architecture must support several operating modes, e.g. primary-secondary. The current implementation of the EU DCCG is, as mentioned previously, a single centralized system that serves as a central platform for storing and managing the necessary information collected from trusted parties.

source_en: The current gateway design is focused on the trust establishment between “National Backends” in terms of a system operated/owned by a national health authority. This can be a script, a fully automated solution or a manual process, which is able to connect the gateway trustfully and able to do uploads and downloads of the content. What other concrete solutions are behind is not in scope of the gateway itself. Within the DDCC scope, the term “National Backend” is worded too sharply, because there can be other parties which can be connected with their publishing system to a gateway in the trust network. Therefore the term “national backend” should be understood within this scope more as “Trusted Party” in terms of an attendee which has received access to a trusted gateway. The trusted gateway or the federator acts then as well as “Trusted Party” to other gateways.
back_translation_en: The current design of the gateway is focused on establishing trust between "national backend systems", in the sense of a system operated/owned by a national health authority. This may be a script, a fully automated solution or a manual process, capable of connecting to the gateway reliably and performing content uploads and downloads. The concrete solutions behind it are outside the scope of the gateway itself. In the DDCC scope, the term "national backend system" is too restrictive, because other parties may be connected with their publishing system to a trust network gateway. Consequently, in this scope, the term "national backend system" should rather be understood as "trusted party", in the sense of a participant that has obtained access to a trust gateway. The trust gateway or the federator then also acts as a "trusted party" vis-à-vis the other gateways.

source_en: To support additional use cases, the gateway will be modified with endpoints which allows it to upload certificates signed by the SCA of a Trust Network Partcipant. The upload endpoint works similar to the signer information upload endpoint with the difference that the upload contains more additional information about the certificate. The concrete template for this additional information must be defined by a schema. The certificate upload must support the choice of a kid, because other standards define static kids or choose it in other ways than the DCC. If no kid is provided, the DCC standard calculation of the first 8 bytes of the SHA256 hash is applied.
back_translation_en: To support additional use cases, the gateway will be modified with endpoints allowing the upload of certificates signed by a trust network participant's SCA. The upload endpoint works similarly to the signer information upload endpoint, except that the upload contains more additional information about the certificate. The concrete model of this additional information must be defined by a schema. Certificate upload must allow the choice of a kid, because other standards define static kids or choose them in a way other than the DCC. If no kid is provided, the standard DCC calculation, namely the first 8 bytes of the SHA256 hash, is applied.

The gateway operators follow a well-documented process to establish the identity and onboard the trust anchor of each Trust Network Participant. The TNG builds on this system to allow the creation of trust gateways by other organizations, which makes it possible to form a federated network of trust gateways supporting all the main COVID-19 credential certificates.
